text.p: About 50 Greenpeace demonstrators protested outside the London headquarters of Anglo-Dutch food manufacturer Unilever on Wednesday as part of a campaign against genetically modified soybeans.
The demonstrators, dressed in white with black X's drawn on their faces, were protesting that consumers had no option to avoid the genetically altered beans from the United States.
"Unilever don't XXXX with us" read a banner strung up on the giant office building on the north bank of the Thames, while sci-fi style music blared in the nearby subway.
"The soybeans will be mixed up with normal beans, so consumers will not be offered a choice and that's just not acceptable," said Mirella Lindenfels, Greenpeace spokeswoman at the demonstration.

The protest followed similar moves in Germany on Tuesday, where German Green party members and consumer and environmental lobbies made a bid to block food products containing the beans or seek labelling of all products using them.
The beans, developed by Monsanto Co, are resistant to a weed-killer and at present account for about two percent of the total U.S. crop.
Greenpeace said it had called on Unilever and other processors and retailers to demand products free of the beans so that consumers can choose not to buy them.
The beans go into products like sausages, ice cream, and vegetable oils.
A Unilever spokesman said it was not possible to separate out the genetically modified beans or label products using them.
"Our position is that we are advised by all concerned that segregation is not possible in terms of large bulk orders."

He said labelling would not be possible either because it would be too difficult to identify where the beans had been used. About 60 percent of all food contains soybeans or soy derivatives. Products such as vegetable oil can sometimes contain soya but sometimes not, he said.
The spokesman said the U.S., UK and European authorities had declared the beans safe and Unilever had come to the same conclusion after making its own assessment.
"There is no reason to be concerned with them," he said.
Europe imports some 14 million tonnes annually from the U.S. and the first batch containing the genetically altered beans is due to arrive in November.
